correctness.rationale: For an aperture shorter than 2N/3, the nonnegative quadratic (1−u)(u+1/2) has mean zero under the two Fourier moment conditions but forces a point mass at u=1, contradicting the first moment. For D=ceil(2N/3), construct three symmetric-radius Lagrange masses with cosine moments (1,0,1/2). Exact algebra shows positive endpoint mass, nonnegative interior masses, and zero two complex moments. All-order bracketing follows from the tangent-factor inequality for N=3k+1 and direct parity bounds otherwise. A real 5×6 affine null vector compresses the six-node precursor to at most five while preserving every moment; neither endpoint can disappear without contradicting the lower bound. At 3|N, the dual polynomial zeros and 3-point DFT prove uniqueness. The extracted standalone code checks 796 residuals at 80 decimal digits for N=3..400; this is corroboration only.

originality.rationale: The assessed claim is the sharp integer consecutive-frequency aperture ceil(2N/3), a five-node positive realization in the same aperture for every N, and the rigid equality classification at divisible orders. Published work on three-site positive Fourier frames optimizes cardinality, and recent cyclotomic work supplies lower-bound mechanisms for a stronger divisibility condition. Neither inspected statement implies the all-order lattice-aperture upper bound. Classical positive-quadrature and general geometric bounds were also compared, with full-text access gaps explicitly retained as residual risks. No database search is taken as proof of uniqueness.

value.rationale: The width of the smallest consecutive frequency window that permits exact, nonnegative reconstruction on three adjacent cyclic sites is an intrinsic finite harmonic-analysis localization invariant, not an arbitrary slice of a table. The exact law ceil(2N/3) is valid in every cyclic order, is independent of prime factors, and is attained with at most five nodes while preserving both endpoints and positivity. It distinguishes bandwidth localization from node count and makes the competing constraints simultaneously feasible at a sharp boundary. The three-atom rigidity when 3 divides N is structural, not a routine isolated numerical example.
